title: Social Facilitation
description: The mere presence of other people improves your performance on easy or well‑practiced tasks but hurts your performance on hard or unfamiliar ones.
shortDescription: The mere presence of other people improves your performance on easy or well‑practiced tasks but hurts your performance on hard or unfamiliar ones.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: The mere presence of other people improves your performance on easy or well‑practiced tasks but hurts your performance on hard or unfamiliar ones.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A musician plays a simple piece flawlessly in front of an audience but fumbles a complex new piece.
An experienced salesperson closes better in a team meeting than alone, but a new hire freezes.
You type faster when a colleague is watching, but you struggle to solve a tricky math problem.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Performing simple routines automatically in front of others.
Choking under pressure on difficult tasks when observed.
Preferring to practice alone, then demonstrate publicly.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “I do better under pressure.” (for easy tasks)
“I can’t think when people are watching.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: Your heart rate increases when someone watches you do something complex.
You feel your mind go blank during a presentation, even though you know the material.
You seek an audience for a well‑rehearsed skill but avoid it for anything new.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: The presence of others increases arousal, which enhances the dominant response. For easy tasks, the dominant response is usually correct; for hard tasks, it’s often incorrect. Robert Zajonc (1965) proposed this explanation, and it has held up well.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Over‑practice difficult tasks until they become easy, then perform publicly.
When learning something new, do it in private until you’ve built the skill.
If you’re a manager, let new hires practice in low‑stakes settings before presenting to leadership.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Forcing a team member to “just present” when they’re not ready, thinking pressure will help. It will hurt.
Assuming you’ll rise to the occasion for something you haven’t practiced.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A junior developer is asked to demo a new feature to a large audience. She’s still shaky on the code. Under the spotlight, her mind goes blank, and she can’t answer basic questions. Later, alone with a colleague, she explains the same feature clearly. The audience amplified her uncertainty.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: An audience is a magnifying glass: it enlarges what’s already there. If you’ve practiced, it makes you better; if you haven’t, it makes you panic.
